SHEET 02 — STOP TREATING IT LIKE A PHONE
02  —  The Premise
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
Before The Settings
Stop Treating It
Like A Phone

I’ve been shooting with dedicated cameras since 2014. For a long time, there was a clear gap between what I could create with my camera and what I could create with my phone.

That gap is still there.

But it’s a lot smaller than it used to be.

Today’s iPhone gives me access to tools and controls that used to exist almost exclusively on dedicated cameras. More importantly, I can apply the same principles I’ve learned behind a camera to something that’s already in my pocket.

That changed the way I look at it.

M02.1
Photo · Primary Stephen shooting on iPhone Portrait 284 × 230 · 5:4
Documentary, not posed — mid-make
Real creator imagery, no product shot
Cinematic Isn’t
A Resolution.
It’s A Series
Of Decisions.
M02.2
Photo · Nuance iPhone beside the pro camera 236 × 144 · both in one kit

4K doesn’t make an image cinematic. Neither does 24 fps, Log, a LUT or a manual camera app.

Those tools give you control. What you do with that control determines the image.

The technology gives you the tools.
You still have to make the image.
The Decisions
01Where is the light coming from?
02How is the frame composed?
03Why is the camera moving?
04What shot comes next?
05What should the color make this feel like?
The Gap Is Closing.
The Ceiling Isn’t The Same.

My professional camera still gives me things the iPhone can’t fully replicate — interchangeable lenses, natural optical depth and files I can push further in post.

I’m not trying to replace that.

I’m trying to use the right camera for the job.

Less Friction.
More Creating.

A full camera setup can give me the image I want, but it takes more time to build, shoot and break down.

My iPhone removes a lot of that friction.

If I can get close to the look I want and create faster, that’s a trade I’ll make.

“I’ll take that gap if I can
scale my content faster.”
— Stephen
Your phone doesn’t need to replace your camera.
You just need to stop treating
it like it isn’t one.

03  —  The Foundation
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
The Foundation
Get Your
iPhone Right

Before you download another app or build out a rig, get the fundamentals right.

Set these once and stop deciding every time you pick up the phone.

Seriously.
Wipe The Lens.
Your phone lives in your hand, your pocket and your bag. Fingerprints soften the image before you press record.

4K / 24
Cinematic Motion
The cadence associated with film. On an iPhone it can feel choppier depending on the shot.
4K / 60
Slow It Down
When I want the option to slow the footage down in the edit.
My practical defaults, not universal requirements
Settings  ›  CameraSet Once
Record Video4K · 30 fps
Grid
HDR VideoLooks wrong off-device and fights the grade
Lock CameraStops the lens switching mid-take
Preserve SettingsCamera Mode
Which Lens To Reach For
1×Main · Default
Best sensor and best low light. Shoot here unless you have a reason not to.
0.5×Ultra Wide
Tight rooms and establishing shots. Keep faces out of the corners.
2–5×Telephoto
Flattering for a talking head. Needs light.
Focal lengths vary by model
Don’t Pick A Frame Rate
Because It Sounds Cinematic.
Pick It For What The Shot
Needs To Do.
From Stephen
Tap your subject to set focus and exposure, then press and hold until it locks. Do it before every take.

The right choice depends on what I’m shooting.

SHEET 05 — BUILD THE IMAGE
05  —  Build The Image
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
The Grade
Build
The Image

Log gives me room. Color correction gets the image back to neutral. The grade is where I decide how I want it to feel.

Those are three different jobs.

Control The Image Before You Grade ItBefore The Color Pass
Frame Rate
Choose it for how the footage needs to move.
Shutter
A starting point is about double the frame rate. 24→1/48, 30→1/60, 60→1/120.
White Balance
If consistency matters, do not let it shift mid-shot. Lock it when your workflow allows.
ISO
As controlled as the scene allows. More ISO is not free light.
ND
Cuts light in bright conditions so you keep the shutter you already chose.
A starting point for natural motion blur, not a rule  ·  [Technical detail to verify]
01Log
Capture Information
Log is supposed to look flat. I am not trying to make the image look finished in camera. I am trying to capture one that gives me more room to work in post.
Protect the image now. Make it pretty later.
M05.1
State 01 Ungraded Apple Log 500 × 155 · straight off the phone
02Corrected
Get Back To Neutral
Before I start building a look, I want the image in a good place. Exposure, white balance, contrast, natural color. Correction is about getting the image right before I start making it mine.
M05.2
State 02 Corrected, not yet graded 500 × 155 · same frame as M05.1
03Graded
Build The Feel
This is the creative pass. The grade should support the mood of the image, not distract from it. I am looking at color, contrast and feel, and deciding how far I actually need to push it.
M05.3
State 03 Final grade 500 × 155 · same frame as M05.1
Color Isn’t There
To Rescue A Bad Image.
It’s There To Finish
A Good One.
Log→Correct→Create
M05.1 to M05.3 must be the same frame from the same take, in three states. Different shots break the argument.

SHEET 06 — SHOOT WITH INTENTION
06  —  Coverage
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
Don’t Just Record It
Shoot With
Intention

Settings can improve the footage. Shot selection makes the video.

Before I press record, I am already thinking about what this shot adds and what I need next.

Grid on. Look at placement, balance, foreground and depth before you hit record.

WMCDMovRev One subject  ·  One light  ·  Six frames
M06.1
Frame 01Wide16:9 · 300 × 169
01 Wide · Set The Scene
Show me where we are. It gives the shots that follow somewhere to live.
M06.2
Frame 02Medium16:9 · 300 × 169
02 Medium · Bring Us Closer
Where natural action and talking-head content lives. Close enough to connect.
M06.3
Frame 03Close16:9 · 300 × 169
03 Close · Create Emphasis
Faces, reactions and key actions carry more weight when you change the scale.
M06.4
Frame 04Detail16:9 · 300 × 169
04 Detail · Show What Matters
Hands, texture, a product, a button being pressed. The part that completes it.
M06.5
Frame 05Movement16:9 · 300 × 169
05 Movement · Move With A Reason
A shot can be static and still be cinematic. Move when the move adds something.
M06.6
Frame 06Reveal16:9 · 300 × 169
06 Reveal · Give The Shot A Payoff
Hide part of the frame, then reveal what matters. It creates depth.
Don’t Collect
Random Pretty Clips.
Collect The Pieces
Of An Edit.
When I am shooting a sequence I am thinking A to Z. What starts the action, what gets us closer, what detail sells it, where movement helps, and what shot finishes the thought.

SHEET 07 — LIGHT + SOUND
07  —  Light & Sound
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
Before More Gear
Light

People will forgive a lot before they will forgive an image they cannot see or audio they cannot understand.

Before I add more gear, I fix the environment.

Start With What’s Already There
Good light can make the iPhone look significantly better before you change another setting. My first move is not always adding a light. It is looking at the light I already have and deciding how to use it.
M07.1
Before Overhead light 221 × 210
No direction, hard shadows
M07.2
After Window light 223 × 210
Same subject, same phone
Moved toward the window
Overhead Light
If overhead lighting is making shadows or color you do not want, turn it off when you can and build around a better source.
Window Light
Move toward it. Use the direction of the light to shape the face instead of just making everything brighter.
Direction
Pay attention to where the light is coming from. Moving yourself or your subject a few feet can completely change the image.
Artificial Light
Add light when the environment is not giving you what you need. The goal is not more light. It is better light.
M07.3
SetupOne light, in use214 × 100
Light The Subject.
Don’t Just Light The Room.
+ Sound
Get The Mic
Closer
The built-in microphones can work when the environment is controlled and the phone is close enough. The farther the phone gets from the person speaking, the more the room becomes part of the recording.
M07.4
Photo iPhone with external audio 164 × 160
Real setup, in use
When Audio Matters
Get the microphone closer to the source.
Reduce environmental noise where you can.
Use an external or wireless microphone when distance, consistency or the room calls for it.
Monitor your audio when your setup allows.
Bad Audio Makes
Good Video Feel Cheap.

SHEET 08 — BUILD THE RIG
08  —  The Kit
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
The Kit
Build
The Rig

You do not need a rig to start. You need one when the friction of not having it costs more than carrying it.

Everything here earns its place by removing a problem I actually had.

01Phone Mount
A cage or a clamp. Something you can hold without covering the lens.
02Tripod
Small and fast to open. The one you will actually bring.
03Microphone
Wireless or shotgun. Closer beats more expensive, every time.
04One Light
A single small panel. You are shaping the light, not flooding the room.
05Power
A battery pack. Recording for a long time will drain the phone.
06Storage
External drive or an offload habit. ProRes fills a phone fast.
What I actually carrySix pieces  ·  One bag

SHEET 09 — THE WORKFLOW
09  —  The Workflow
Your iPhone Is A Cinema CameraField Guide 001
The Loop
The
Workflow

The gear question is the one everybody asks. It is almost never the one holding them back.

Six stages. The same six, every time, until you stop having to think about them.

Stage 01
Shoot
Get coverage, not takes. Wide, medium, close, before the camera moves.
Stage 02
Offload
Off the phone the same day. Your camera roll is not an archive.
Stage 03
Select
Watch it once. Mark what works. Do not start cutting yet.
Stage 04
Cut
Structure first. Nothing gets polished before the shape is right.
Stage 05
Color
Correct, then grade. In that order, every single time.
Stage 06
Ship
The version that goes out beats the one you keep improving.
Back to 01
Most People Don’t Have
A Camera Problem.
They Have A
Workflow Problem.
— Stephen
M09.1
Screenshot The edit, mid-cut 316 × 154 · your real timeline
Stage 04, before color
Run the same six stages until they stop being decisions and start being habits.
